facts.statement: A biomechanical study suggests that running at high speeds may have been impossible for Acrocanthosaurus.
facts.quote: The finding may mean that running was also not possible for other giant theropod dinosaurs like Giganotosaurus, Mapusaurus and Acrocanthosaurus

facts.statement: There were nineteen curved, serrated teeth on each side of the upper jaw of Acrocanthosaurus.
facts.quote: Nineteen curved, serrated teeth lined each side of the upper jaw

facts.statement: The lower neural spines of Acrocanthosaurus had muscle attachments similar to modern bison, likely forming a tall, thick ridge along its back.
facts.quote: The lower spines of Acrocanthosaurus had attachments for powerful muscles like those of modern bison, probably forming a tall, thick ridge down its back.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus vertebrae featured prominent depressions called pleurocoels on the sides of the neck and back bones, with smaller ones on the tail bones.
facts.quote: All of its cervical (neck) and dorsal (back) vertebrae had prominent depressions (pleurocoels) on the sides, while the caudal (tail) vertebrae bore smaller ones.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus was a bipedal dinosaur with a long, heavy tail that balanced its head and body over its hips.
facts.quote: Acrocanthosaurus was bipedal, with a long, heavy tail counterbalancing the head and body, maintaining its center of gravity over its hips.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus had shorter and more robust forelimbs than Allosaurus, with each hand containing three clawed digits.
facts.quote: Its forelimbs were relatively shorter and more robust than those of Allosaurus but were otherwise similar: each hand bore three clawed digits.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus had a femur longer than its tibia and metatarsals, suggesting it was not a fast runner.
facts.quote: Unlike many smaller fast-running dinosaurs, its femur was longer than its tibia and metatarsals, suggesting that Acrocanthosaurus was not a fast runner.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus feet had four digits, with the first digit being much smaller and not touching the ground.
facts.quote: Its feet had four digits each, although, as is typical for theropods, the first was much smaller than the rest and did not make contact with the ground.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus is classified within the superfamily Allosauroidea and the infraorder Tetanurae.
facts.quote: Acrocanthosaurus is classified in the superfamily Allosauroidea within the infraorder Tetanurae.

facts.statement: Most scientific studies classify Acrocanthosaurus as a member of the family Carcharodontosauridae.
facts.quote: Most studies have found it to be a member of the related family Carcharodontosauridae.

facts.statement: Alfred Sherwood Romer transferred Acrocanthosaurus to the family Megalosauridae in 1956, after it had initially been assigned to Antrodemidae by J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston Jr.
facts.quote: J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston Jr. first assigned it to the "Antrodemidae", the equivalent of the Allosauridae, but it was transferred to the Megalosauridae, a wastebasket taxon, by Alfred Sherwood Romer in 1956.

facts.statement: Some researchers and books from the 1980s interpreted Acrocanthosaurus as a member of the family Spinosauridae based on its tall vertebrae.
facts.quote: This interpretation of Acrocanthosaurus as a spinosaurid persisted into the 1980s, and was repeated in the semi-technical dinosaur books of the time.

facts.statement: In 1988, Gregory S. Paul named a second species, A. altispinax, based on tall spined vertebrae from England that were thought to be similar to Acrocanthosaurus.
facts.quote: Tall spined vertebrae from the Early Cretaceous of England were once considered to be very similar to those of Acrocanthosaurus, and in 1988 Gregory S. Paul named them as a second species of the genus, A. altispinax.

facts.statement: Bone features suggest Acrocanthosaurus required at least 12 years to reach full maturity.
facts.quote: From the bone features of the holotype OMNH 10146 and NCSM 14345, it is estimated that Acrocanthosaurus required at least 12 years to fully grow.

facts.statement: When accounting for lost growth lines, Acrocanthosaurus likely needed 18 to 24 years to reach maturity.
facts.quote: If accounting for these lines, then Acrocanthosaurus needed 18–24 years to be mature.

facts.statement: Studies estimate Acrocanthosaurus had a bite force of 8,266 newtons at the front of the jaws and 16,894 newtons at the back.
facts.quote: According to the results, its bite force at the anterior part of the jaws was 8,266 newtons, while the posterior bite force was estimated to be 16,894 newtons.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus forelimbs did not touch the ground and were not used for walking.
facts.quote: Like those of most other non-avian theropods, Acrocanthosaurus forelimbs did not make contact with the ground and were not used for locomotion

facts.statement: A complete forelimb specimen, identified as NCSM 14345, was discovered and used to analyze the arm's function and movement.
facts.quote: The discovery of a complete forelimb (NCSM 14345) allowed the first analysis of the function and range of motion of the forelimb in Acrocanthosaurus

facts.statement: Bone surfaces in the forelimb joints did not fit precisely, suggesting significant cartilage was present to allow movement.
facts.quote: In many of the joints, the bones did not fit together exactly, indicating the presence of a considerable amount of cartilage in the joints

facts.statement: The Acrocanthosaurus arm could retract 109 degrees backward from the vertical position.
facts.quote: The arm could not swing in a complete circle, but could retract (swing backward) 109° from the vertical

facts.statement: The Acrocanthosaurus arm could only swing forward 24 degrees past the vertical.
facts.quote: Protraction (swinging forward) was limited to only 24° past the vertical

facts.statement: The arm could not straighten completely or bend far enough to form a right angle between the upper arm and forearm.
facts.quote: The arm could not completely extend (straighten), nor could it flex (bend) very far, with the humerus unable even to form a right angle with the forearm

facts.statement: The radius and ulna bones were locked together, preventing the twisting motion seen in human forearms.
facts.quote: The radius and ulna (forearm bones) locked together so that there was no possibility of pronation or supination (twisting) as in human forearms

facts.statement: The forelimbs could not reach forward far enough to scratch the animal's own neck.
facts.quote: The forelimbs could not swing forward very far, unable even to scratch the animal's own neck

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Acrocanthosaurus likely used its mouth rather than its forelimbs to initially capture prey.
facts.quote: Therefore, they were not likely to have been used in the initial capture of prey and Acrocanthosaurus probably led with its mouth when hunting

facts.statement: It is hypothesized that Acrocanthosaurus used its forelimbs to hold prey against its body after the jaws seized it.
facts.quote: Once prey had been seized in the jaws, the heavily muscled forelimbs may have retracted, holding the prey tightly against the body and preventing escape

facts.statement: Some theories suggest Acrocanthosaurus could climb sauropods to topple them, but this is considered unlikely due to its robust leg structure.
facts.quote: Other less probable theories have suggested the forelimb range of motion being able to grasp onto the side of a sauropod and clinging on to topple the sauropods of smaller stature, though this is unlikely due to Acrocanthosaurus having a rather robust leg structure compared to other similarly structured theropods

facts.statement: In 2005, scientists used CT scanning to create an endocast of the holotype braincase, identified as OMNH 10146.
facts.quote: In 2005, scientists reconstructed an endocast (replica) of an Acrocanthosaurus cranial cavity using computed tomography (CT scanning) to analyze the spaces within the holotype braincase (OMNH 10146)

facts.statement: The brain structure resembles Carcharodontosaurus and Giganotosaurus more than Allosaurus or Sinraptor, supporting the hypothesis that Acrocanthosaurus was a carcharodontosaurid.
facts.quote: It most resembles the brains of Carcharodontosaurus and Giganotosaurus rather than those of Allosaurus or Sinraptor, providing support for the hypothesis that Acrocanthosaurus was a carcharodontosaurid

facts.statement: Large olfactory bulbs indicate that Acrocanthosaurus had a good sense of smell.
facts.quote: Acrocanthosaurus had large and bulbous olfactory bulbs, indicating a good sense of smell

facts.statement: Analysis of the ear canals suggests the head was held at a 25-degree angle below horizontal.
facts.quote: Reconstructing the semicircular canals of the ear, which control balance, shows that the head was held at a 25° angle below horizontal

facts.statement: Large, three-toed theropod footprints are preserved in the Glen Rose Formation of central Texas.
facts.quote: The Glen Rose Formation of central Texas preserves many dinosaur footprints, including large, three-toed theropod prints

facts.statement: It is debated whether the overlapping footprints indicate a pack of Acrocanthosaurus stalking sauropods, as other explanations exist.
facts.quote: This has been put forth as evidence that a small pack of Acrocanthosaurus was stalking a herd of sauropods. While interesting and plausible, this hypothesis is difficult to prove and other explanations exist

facts.statement: The holotype skull shows light exostotic material on the squamosal bone.
facts.quote: The skull of the Acrocanthosaurus atokensis holotype shows light exostotic material on the squamosal

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus lived during the Aptian and Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Therefore, Acrocanthosaurus most likely existed between 125 and 99.6 million years ago.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus lived in North America during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically the Albian stage.
facts.quote: que existió a finales del período Cretácico Inferior, de entre 125 million years ago, durante el Albiense, en lo que hoy es Norteamérica.

facts.statement: The habitat of Acrocanthosaurus included large floodplains that drained into shallow inland seas.
facts.quote: During this time, the area preserved in the Twin Mountains and Antlers formations was a large floodplain that drained into a shallow inland sea.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus was capable of spreading across the continent before the Western Interior Seaway formed.
facts.quote: The presence of Acrocanthosaurus in the Arundel Formation suggests that it had managed to spread across the continent before the seaway could impede it.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus inhabited coastal environments, including mudflats along ancient shorelines.
facts.quote: The Glen Rose Formation represents a coastal environment, with possible Acrocanthosaurus tracks preserved in mudflats along the ancient shoreline.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus was a bipedal predator known for high neural spines along its vertebrae that supported a hump over its neck, back, and hips.
facts.quote: El Acrocanthosaurus era un depredador bípedo, y como el nombre indica, se lo conoce principalmente por sus apófisis espinosa, ubicadas en muchas de sus vértebras, y que parecen haber sostenido una «joroba» encima del cuello, espalda y caderas del animal.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus was one of the largest theropods, reaching nearly 12 meters in length and weighing between 5.7 and 6.2 tonnes.
facts.quote: El acrocantosaurio fue uno de los terópodos más grandes, de casi 12 metros de longitud y un peso de entre 5.7 a 6.2 toneladas.

facts.statement: The largest and most complete specimen, NCSM 14345, is estimated to be 11.5 meters long, weigh between 5.7 and 6.2 tonnes, and have a skull approximately 1.3 meters long.
facts.quote: El individuo más grande y completo que se ha descubierto, NCSM 14345 se estima que su longitud fue de 11,5 metros y con un peso estimado de 5,7 a 6,2 toneladas, con un rango máximo de 7,25 toneladas posibles para el espécimen y su cráneo medía aproximadamente 1,3 metros de largo.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus is distinguished by a row of high neural spines running from the neck to the end of the tail, measuring up to 2.5 times the height of the vertebra.
facts.quote: Lo que más destaca al acrocantosaurio es su fila de altas espinas neurales que se localizan en las vértebras desde el cuello hasta el final de la cola, midiendo hasta 2,5 veces la altura de la vértebra.

facts.statement: The function of the neural spines is unknown, but they likely served for communication, fat storage, or thermoregulation.
facts.quote: La función de estas espinas permanece desconocida, aunque probablemente pudieron servir para la comunicación, almacenamiento de grasa, o termorregulación.

facts.statement: The leg bones of Acrocanthosaurus were more robust than those of its smaller relative, Allosaurus.
facts.quote: No es de sorprender que los huesos de las patas del acrocantosaurio eran más robustos que los de su pequeño pariente el alosaurio.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus was not a fast runner, as its femur was longer than its tibia and metatarsus.
facts.quote: A diferencia de muchos dinosaurios veloces más pequeños, el fémur era más largo que la tibia y el metatarso, demostrando que el acrocantosaurio no era un rápido corredor.

facts.statement: Acrocanthosaurus is classified in the family Carcharodontosauridae.

facts.quote: species_authority: Stovall & Langston, 1950

facts.statement: There is an ongoing debate regarding the evolutionary relationships of Acrocanthosaurus, with some scientists classifying it as an allosaurid and others as a carcharodontosaurid.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, persiste el debate sobre sus relaciones evolutivas, mientras que algunos científicos lo clasifican como un alosáurido, otros en cambio sostienen que es un carcarodontosáurido.

facts.statement: Large fossil footprints found in Texas may belong to Acrocanthosaurus, though they have not been directly associated with skeletons.
facts.quote: Grandes huellas fósiles descubiertas en Texas pudieron pertenecer al acrocantosaurio, aunque no se las ha asociado directamente con esqueletos.

facts.statement: The name Acrocanthosaurus refers to its high neural spines, derived from Greek words meaning 'high', 'spine', and 'lizard'.
facts.quote: Acrocanthosaurus fue nombrado por sus altas espinas neurales, del griego ακρα/akra ("alta"), ακανθα/akantha ("espina") y σαυρος/sauros ("lagarto").

facts.statement: Only one species, A. atokensis, has been described, named after Atoka County in Oklahoma where the first specimens were found.
facts.quote: Solo hay una especie descrita (A. atokensis), nombrada por el condado de Atoka en Oklahoma, donde los primeros especímenes fueron encontrados.

facts.statement: The name was coined in 1950 by American paleontologists J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston, Jr.
facts.quote: El nombre fue acuñado en 1950 por los paleontólogos estadounidenses J. Willis Stovall y Wann Langston, Jr.

facts.statement: Langston proposed the name 'Acracanthus atokaensis' in his unpublished 1947 master's thesis, but it was changed to Acrocanthosaurus atokensis in the formal publication.
facts.quote: Langston propuso el nombre «Acracanthus atokaensis» en su tesis inédita de maestría de 1947, pero el nombre se cambió a Acrocanthosaurus atokensis en la publicación formal.

facts.statement: The holotype and paratype, OMNH 10146 and OMNH 10147 respectively, were discovered in the early 1940s and described simultaneously in 1950.
facts.quote: El holotipo y paratipo, OMNH 10146 y OMNH 10147 respectivamente, fueron descubiertos a principios de la década de 1940 y descritos al mismo tiempo en 1950

facts.statement: The holotype and paratype consist of two incomplete individuals with skull remains found in the Antlers Formation in Oklahoma.
facts.quote: consisten en dos individuos incompletos con restos del cráneo, encontrados en la Formación Antlers en Oklahoma.

facts.statement: Two much more complete specimens were described in the 1990s.
facts.quote: Dos ejemplares mucho más completos fueron descritos en la década de 1990.

facts.statement: The first complete specimen, SMU 74646, is a partial skeleton lacking much of the skull and was excavated in the Twin Mountain Formation in Texas.
facts.quote: El primero, SMU 74646 es un esqueleto parcial, que carece de gran parte del cráneo, que fue excavado en la Formación Twin Mountain en Texas

facts.statement: The most complete skeleton, NCSM 14345, nicknamed 'Fran', was also found in the Antlers Formation by private collectors.
facts.quote: Y el más completo de los esqueletos, NCSM 14345, apodado «Fran», fue hallado también en la Formación de Antlers por coleccionistas privados

facts.statement: This is the largest specimen discovered to date and possesses the only complete skull and arm.
facts.quote: Este es el espécimen más grande descubierto hasta ahora y posee el único cráneo y brazo completo.

facts.statement: The presence of Acrocanthosaurus in the Cloverly Formation was established in 2012 with the description of another partial skeleton, UM 20796.
facts.quote: La presencia de Acrocanthosaurus en la Formación Cloverly se estableció en 2012 con la descripción de otro esqueleto parcial, UM 20796.

facts.statement: This specimen, consisting of parts of two vertebrae, partial pubic bones, a femur, partial fibula, and various fragments, represents a juvenile animal.
facts.quote: Este ejemplar, que consta de partes de dos vértebras, huesos púbicos parciales, un fémur, peroné parcial, y fragmentos varios, representa un animal juvenil.

facts.statement: It comes from a bone bed in the Bighorn Basin of north-central Wyoming and was found near the shoulder blade of a Sauroposeidon.
facts.quote: Proviene de una cama de huesos en la cuenca Bighorn del centro-norte de Wyoming, y fue encontrado cerca del omóplato de un Sauroposeidon.

facts.statement: A tooth from southern Arizona has been assigned to this genus, and tooth marks have been found on bones of a sauropod from the same area.
facts.quote: Un diente del sur de Arizona ha sido asignado a este género, y marcas de dientes han sido halladas en huesos de un saurópodo de la misma área.

facts.statement: Several teeth from the Arundel Formation in Maryland have been identified as belonging to Acrocanthosaurus, indicating a possible distribution to the far east of North America.
facts.quote: Varios dientes de la Formación de Arundel en Maryland han sido identificados con los del acrocantosaurio e indican una posible distribución hasta el extremo este de Norteamérica.

facts.statement: In 2022, several footprints (ichnofossils) of this theropod were discovered in Dinosaur Valley, Texas, as a result of intense drought in this region of the United States.
facts.quote: En el 2022, varias huellas (icnofósil) de este terópodo fueron descubiertas en el Valle de los Dinosaurios, (Texas), como consecuencia de una intensa sequía en esta región de Estados Unidos

facts.statement: This caused a riverbed to dry up, revealing nearly 60 impressions (estimated at a total of 140) over a 30-meter stretch, with an age of 113 million years.
facts.quote: lo que provocó que el lecho de un río se secara y quedaran al descubierto cerca de 60 impresiones (estimándose un total de 140) en un trayecto de 30 metros, con una antigüedad de 113 millones de años
